title: The Pledges at al-Aqabah
year: The pilgrimage seasons of the 11th to 13th years of prophethood — 620 CE to June 622 CE
era: The Pledge That Named Its Price
teaser: Twice they were warned to walk away — lost property, murdered nobles. They asked only: what is our reward?

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Six men at Mina, from a city at war with itself
layers.content:
The Prophet ﷺ worked the pilgrimage season like a man with one door still open. Al-Mubarakpuri describes the method plainly: he met the delegations of the Arabian tribes by night, so that the hostile Makkans could not get between him and them. In the eleventh year of prophethood he sat with Bani Dhuhal, Ali and Abu Bakr beside him. The conversation went well and the tribe suspended its decision.

Then, passing al-Aqabah at Mina, he heard voices and turned towards them. Six men from Yathrib, all of them of Khazraj: As'ad bin Zurarah, Awf bin al-Harith, Rafi' bin Malik, Qutbah bin Amir, Uqbah bin Amir and Jabir bin Abdullah. Ibn Sa'd places the meeting at the pilgrimage of 620 CE and records that Musa ibn Uqba counted eight men rather than six, with a partly different list. Reports differ on exactly who was standing there.

The opening is short enough to quote whole. Who are you? From the tribe of Khazraj. Are you the allies of the Jews? Yes. Then why not sit down for a little, and I will speak to you.

They sat, and what held them was not curiosity. Their Jewish neighbours in Yathrib had been telling them for years that a prophet was due, and had used it as a threat — that when he came they would follow him and finish their enemies with him. The six put it to each other in those terms: this is the prophet the Jews keep holding over us, so let us be the first to reach him.

They accepted Islam, and the reason they gave had nothing to do with Makkah. No tribe, they said, is so divided by hate and enmity as ours. Allah may cement our ties through you. Then they went home to argue for it.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: What Happened
layers.subtitle: Terms with no war in them, and one teacher sent north
layers.content:
The next pilgrimage, in the twelfth year of prophethood, twelve men came down from Yathrib. Five of the original six returned; the one who stayed away was Jabir bin Abdullah bin Ri'ab. The seven new men were Mu'adh bin al-Harith, Dhakwan bin Abdul-Qais, Ubadah bin as-Samit, Yazeed bin Tha'labah and al-Abbas bin Ubadah bin Nadlah of Khazraj, with Abul-Haitham bin at-Taihan and Uwaim bin Sa'idah of Aws. Ibn Sa'd counts them as ten of Khazraj and two of Aws. It is the first time the other tribe of the city is in the room.

Al-Bukhari keeps the terms in the narration of Ubadah bin as-Samit. Come and pledge that you will not associate any with Allah, nor steal, nor commit unlawful sexual intercourse, nor kill your children, nor utter slander you have forged, nor disobey me in what is good. Whoever fulfils it, Allah will reward him. Whoever falls short and is punished for it in this world may find that punishment his redemption. And if the sin stays hidden and no grief reaches him, his affair is with Allah — He may forgive him, or He may not.

Then they asked for a teacher, and he sent Mus'ab bin Umair, who lodged with As'ad bin Zurarah. One man, no protection, one year.

It was enough. When Usaid bin Hudair came at Mus'ab with a spear, cursing, Mus'ab invited him to sit and told him he was free to keep clear of the message if he found it objectionable. Usaid drove his lance into the sand, listened, heard verses of the Qur'an, and asked what a man does to enter this religion. He then fetched Sa'd bin Mu'adh, whose people would follow wherever he went, and the scene repeated itself. By that evening every man and woman of those two clans had accepted Islam but one — al-Usairim, who held back until the day of Uhud, then accepted Islam, fought, and was killed before he had made a single prostration in prayer. He has done a little, the Prophet ﷺ said of him, but his reward is great.

Mus'ab kept at it until there were Muslims in every house of the Ansar.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ubadah bin as-Samit — the terms of the First Pledge of al-Aqabah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 1/431-438; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: Seventy-three men, two women, and the cost read out twice
layers.content:
The thirteenth year of prophethood, June 622 CE. Over seventy believers came to the pilgrimage in the same caravan as their own idolaters, repeating one question among themselves: is it not high time that we protect Muhammad instead of leaving him abandoned and stumbling in the hillocks of Makkah?

They set a night in the middle of the days of Tashreeq, at the same hillock. Ka'b bin Malik, who was there, gave the account. They slept with their people, and after a third of the night had gone they slipped out — Ibn Sa'd says hidden like sand-grouse — seventy-three men and two women, Nusaibah bint Ka'b of Bani Mazin bin Najjar and Asma' bint Amr of Bani Salamah.

The Prophet ﷺ came with his uncle al-Abbas, still on the religion of his people, who spoke first — and spoke against the deal. If you can carry what you are promising, take the burden. But if you mean to surrender him and betray him after taking him away, leave him now; he is respected and well defended where he is.

Ka'b answered for him: we have heard your words; now speak, Messenger of Allah, and take from us any pledge you wish.

The articles, in the narration of Jabir recorded by Imam Ahmad: to listen and obey in hardship and ease; to spend in plenty and in scarcity; to enjoin good and forbid evil; to fear the censure of no one in Allah's service; to aid him when he comes to them, and protect him as they would protect their own wives and children.

Then al-Abbas bin Ubadah priced it. You are affirming that you will fight the world. If you fear for your property, or for the lives of your nobles, leave him now. They answered that they had already counted the loss of property and the murder of their notables, and asked one question: what is our reward if we keep every item of this pact? Paradise, he said. Extend your hand. They pledged man by man. The two women pledged orally, for he never took the hand of an unrelated woman.
layers.hadith_ref: Musnad Ahmad, narrated by Jabir — the articles of the Second Pledge, with a good chain, graded authentic by al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban; the oral pledge of the two women — Sahih Muslim
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 1/440-447 and Musnad Ahmad 3/322; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: No ayah for these nights, and the wording that outlived them
layers.content:
No revelation is recorded as coming down about either night at al-Aqabah, and that should be stated plainly rather than filled in. What the Qur'an holds is the wording.

The terms taken in the first pledge are the terms of the ayah on receiving the allegiance of believing women: «إِذَا جَاءَكَ الْمُؤْمِنَاتُ يُبَايِعْنَكَ عَلَىٰ أَن لَّا يُشْرِكْنَ بِاللَّهِ شَيْئًا وَلَا يَسْرِقْنَ وَلَا يَزْنِينَ وَلَا يَقْتُلْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ» — 'when the believing women come to you, pledging that they will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit unlawful intercourse, nor kill their children.' (60:12) That is why Ibn Sa'd records the first night's other name, bay'at an-nisa': the list contains no fighting.

The second night was a different instrument, and Ibn Sa'd names it too — bay'at al-harb, the Pledge of War, because it added fighting to obedience. Permission for that came later and separately, and the Qur'an gave it its own verse: «أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَاتَلُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا» — 'Permission to fight is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged.' (22:39)

What no verse covered, he settled with his own word. Abul-Haitham raised the risk out loud that night: between us and the Jews there are agreements we would be severing, and if Allah gives you victory, will you go back to your own people? The Prophet ﷺ smiled. Your blood will be my blood; I will fight whom you fight and make peace with whom you make peace.

One more thing was settled before the gathering broke up, and it was structural. The Prophet ﷺ asked them to appoint twelve representatives, nine of Khazraj and three of Aws, and took a further undertaking from those twelve: you are responsible over your people in the matters among them, a responsibility like that of the disciples of Isa bin Maryam, and I am responsible over my people. They agreed.

A city that had no Muslim in it two years earlier now had named men answerable for it.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 60:12 — the terms on which the allegiance of believing women is received; Quran 22:39 — «أُذِنَ لِلَّذِينَ يُقَاتَلُونَ بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا» permission to fight, given later
layers.hadith_ref: The charge to the twelve representatives — al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: A shout from the high ground, and a road that opened
layers.content:
It ended badly and then well. A voice went up from the highest ground: people of the dwellings, Muhammad and his renegades have gathered to make war on you. The Prophet ﷺ named the caller as the jinn of al-Aqabah, told him they were leaving, and ordered everyone back to their camps.

Al-Abbas bin Ubadah — the same man who had spent the night explaining how expensive the pact would be — offered to put the people of Mina to the sword by morning. We have not been commanded to follow that course, he said. Go back to your camps.

Quraysh arrived at the Madinese camp the next day to protest that a treaty had been made to take Muhammad out of the city. The idolaters of the caravan, who knew nothing, swore in good faith that there was no truth in it, and Abdullah bin Ubai denounced the report, saying his people would never act without his orders. The Muslims among them said nothing. Quraysh went home unsatisfied, kept scrutinising, and established the truth only after the pilgrims had left. Then they rode after them and caught one man — Sa'd bin Ubadah, whom they tortured until two Makkans he had traded with pulled him out of their hands.

Afterwards it was called the Great Pledge of al-Aqabah. Al-Mubarakpuri's judgement is that a small Muslim state now existed in a desert of disbelief, and the consequence was immediate: the Prophet ﷺ gave the Muslims leave to migrate, and the road north opened.

Note what the pledge did not say. Al-Mubarakpuri points out that its clauses bound the Ansar to defend him where they lived, not to fight beyond their own territory — which is why, on the road to Badr, he had to put the question to them again and wait for an answer.

They were told the price twice, by two different men, and invited both times to walk away. They asked what the reward was, and then put out their hands. A commitment made after the bill has been read aloud is a different object from one made in enthusiasm, and it is the only kind that survives contact with the cost.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam, citing Ibn Hisham 1/447-450 and Zadul-Ma'ad 2/51-52

quiz.prompt: Why is the First Pledge of al-Aqabah also known as bay'at an-nisa', the Pledge of the Women?

options.text: Because two women were among the twelve who gave it
Because it contained no undertaking to fight, and these are the terms usually taken from women
Because it was given at night, away from the men of Quraysh
Because the women of Madinah accepted Islam before the men

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The list in al-Bukhari's narration from Ubadah bin as-Samit is entirely moral: no shirk, no theft, no unlawful intercourse, no killing of children, no forged slander, no disobedience in what is good. War is not in it.

quiz.prompt: Whom did the Prophet ﷺ send to Madinah after the First Pledge, and what was his task?

options.text: Abu Bakr, to negotiate protection with the chiefs of Aws and Khazraj
Ali bin Abi Talib, to prepare a house for the migration
Mus'ab bin Umair, to teach the Qur'an and the obligations of the religion
Zayd bin Harithah, to carry letters to the Jewish tribes

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He went as a teacher, not as an envoy of state. Within a year, al-Mubarakpuri records, there were Muslims in every house of the Ansar.

quiz.prompt: How did Mus'ab respond when Usaid bin Hudair came at him with a spear and ordered him to stop preaching?

options.text: He invited him to sit and listen, and said he was free to keep clear of it if he found it objectionable
He called on As'ad's clan to protect him under tribal law
He warned him of the punishment awaiting those who obstruct the message
He left the gathering and continued elsewhere in the city

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: That is fair, Usaid said, then drove his lance into the sand and sat down. The conversion of two clans turns on an offer that carried no pressure at all.

quiz.prompt: How many people gave the Second Pledge at al-Aqabah?

options.text: Twelve men, the same delegation as the year before
Forty men of Aws and Khazraj
Seventy-three men and two women
Three hundred, the whole Madinese caravan

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the account of Ka'b bin Malik; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nusaibah bint Ka'b and Asma' bint Amr. The men pledged by hand, one at a time. The pledge of the two women was taken orally.

quiz.prompt: Abul-Haitham asked what would happen to Madinah if Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ victory — would he return to his own people? What was the answer?

options.text: That the matter was with Allah and could not be promised
That he would return to Makkah, but Madinah would keep its treaties
That the question itself showed a weakness of faith
'Your blood will be my blood. I will fight whom you fight and make peace with whom you make peace'

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Ishaq in Ibn Hisham
quiz.scholar_reflection: The question was about treaties they would have to break and the cost of siding with him. Al-Mubarakpuri records that the Prophet ﷺ smiled before answering.

quiz.prompt: Al-Abbas, the Prophet's own uncle and not yet a Muslim, spoke first that night — and argued them out of the pledge rather than into it. What do you make of that?

options.text: A commitment worth having has to survive someone talking you out of it
He was doing what family does: making sure his nephew was not handed to strangers
It made the pledge legally serious rather than emotionally warm
He had no faith in the message and complete concern for the man

quiz.slider_label: Do you want your commitments tested before you make them?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the speech of al-Abbas bin Abdul-Muttalib at al-Aqabah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Leave him now, he told them, because he is respected and well defended where he is. No one in that hollow could later say they had not been warned.

quiz.prompt: They were told the pact meant lost property and murdered nobles. Their reply was a question: what is our reward? What does that exchange say about how they were thinking?

options.text: They had done the arithmetic before they arrived, and it was already settled
Asking about the reward is not mercenary — it is asking what the loss is for
Naming the cost aloud is what turned a mood into a contract
They wanted the terms in the open so nobody could later say they had been misled

quiz.slider_label: How honestly do you count the cost before you commit?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Ishaq — the warning of al-Abbas bin Ubadah bin Nadlah
quiz.scholar_reflection: We have already considered the loss of property and the murder of our notables, they said, and we pay him allegiance. Then: what is our reward? The answer was one word.

quiz.prompt: One man teaching in Madinah for a year changed a city more than a decade of confrontation in Makkah had. What accounts for the difference?

options.text: The ground was different — a divided city was looking for something to unite it
Mus'ab was not competing for authority there, and in Makkah the message was
Teaching quietly reaches people that public argument only hardens
Their neighbours had spent years telling them a prophet was coming

quiz.slider_label: Do you persuade better in public or one to one?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the mission of Mus'ab bin Umair in Madinah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Mubarakpuri's phrase is that the ground was well-prepared. Neither reading works alone: the seed and the soil are both in the account.

quiz.prompt: Offered the chance to put the people of Mina to the sword the next morning, the Prophet ﷺ said: we have not been commanded to follow that course. What is being held in check there?

options.text: Capability is not permission — the limit is the command, not the odds
He refused the first fight on offer while accepting a pledge that promised fighting later
Restraint at the moment of maximum provocation is the whole test
It kept the pledge from beginning as a raid, which is how it would have been remembered

quiz.slider_label: How well do you sit on a capability you are free to use?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, citing Ibn Hisham — the night al-Aqabah was exposed
quiz.scholar_reflection: The offer came from al-Abbas bin Ubadah, who had spent that same night explaining to everyone how costly the pact would be. He was not bluffing.

quiz.prompt: The pledge bound the Ansar to defend him in their own city — not to fight outside it. Before Badr he had to ask them again. What does a clearly bounded promise tell you?

options.text: A promise with edges is more trustworthy than one without them
He read the limits of his own agreement honestly rather than stretching them
What they gave later was a second, freely given commitment, not the first one enforced
Knowing exactly what you agreed to is what makes going beyond it mean anything

quiz.slider_label: Do you keep the letter of what you promised, or the mood of it?
quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — 'the clauses of the Pledge of al-Aqabah did not commit them to fighting beyond their territories'
quiz.scholar_reflection: He could have treated the pledge as a blank cheque. Instead he asked the Helpers for their view and waited for the answer.
